title: Cut and Name
context: Grade 4, the first working topic of the fractions chapter. An adult sees a shape being shaded in, which a child could do with a pencil. What is actually being settled is which of the two written numbers does which job, and that equal is part of the meaning rather than a tidiness rule. A child who reads the pair as two ordinary numbers will go on to say that three eighths beats three quarters, and will say it with confidence, because eight is the larger number.

writeup.why: Cut one whole into equal parts, take some of them, and find out which of the two numbers of a fraction does which job.
writeup.look: One whole thing in the middle of the stage with a cutter above it, an empty fraction being filled in underneath, and five labelled trays along the foot.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Cut and Name' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the parts coloured against the parts the whole was cut into, two numbers in ink one above the other in the same arrangement as the fraction being built, so the corner is read the same way round as the work. On the third phase it carries the cards sorted against the cards in the stack. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The whole sits across the top of the working area inside a mat 800 by 300 at 207,202, and it is switchable between a long bar 720 by 150, a circle of radius 132 and a row of separate counters of one kind. The cutter dial is 240 by 56 at 487,150, reading from two up to twenty. Turning it draws every cut as a near-black line right across the whole BEFORE anything can be filled, so the lower number can be counted on an empty bar, and the cuts go in at measured equal spacing with the outermost pieces the same width as the inner ones. Tapping a part fills it deep blue and raises the upper count; a part that has not been taken keeps its amber and its full size and is never faded, cropped or pushed off the mat. The empty fraction stands under the mat at 487,520, an upper slot 120 by 76 above a level rule 160 by 6 above a lower slot 120 by 76, filled by dragging number tiles into them. When both slots hold a tile the mat runs a counting pass over itself, ticking the cut lines against the lower slot from left to right and then the filled parts against the upper slot, with nothing marked either way and the child's tiles left exactly where they were put. The free cut control replaces the even cutter with one draggable line: while the two pieces differ a measuring bar runs along each of them and prints its length, the naming slots refuse every tile and print what is wrong with the picture rather than what the answer is, and an evenly cut copy of the same whole is drawn directly beneath from the same left edge. The collection view swaps the cut whole for a row of identical separate things and keeps the same fraction underneath it. The shelf runs along the foot of the working area, 1086 by 120 at 64,598, five trays 200 by 96 reading proper, improper, like, unlike and unit, with the card stack beside it. A card may be dropped into more than one tray and every tray it earns stays open; a tray it has not earned slides the card back with nothing marked and lights the two numbers that tray compares. Cards sharing a lower number are drawn shoulder to shoulder wherever they land. Cut again divides one chosen piece in two and rewrites the label under every piece on the mat. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a slot has to be filled, and on the second and third phases a word pad of this chapter's own words, half, quarter, equal parts, proper, improper, like, unlike and unit, so a picture can be named and a tray called with one press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the parts a fraction counts are deep blue, the parts of that same whole which it leaves are amber, a whole shown entire or a bracket spanning one whole is green, a second writing of an amount already on the stage is rose, the greater of two fractions one of the chapter's rules can settle is vermilion, and a pair neither rule settles is sky blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told from the rest by the drawn cut between them and by the label under it before it is ever told by a fill, and every cut, score line, cell edge and guide line is near-black. A fraction is drawn everywhere with its upper number above a level horizontal line and its lower number below, both upright and centred; the line is never slanted and the two numbers are never set side by side. Nothing on this mat is ever shaded without being cut first. A whole that has not been through the cutter has no fill available to it at all, because a filled shape with no cuts in it shows an amount and hides the very number the child is here to read.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last whole the child cut, its uncounted parts still drawn, the fraction written underneath, and the trays each of the sorted cards landed in.

phases.win: both slots fill, and the cuts and the coloured parts are counted back against the picture
phases.does: sets the number of cuts, colours some of the parts, then fills the two slots
phases.goal: the lower number counts the equal parts and the upper number counts the parts taken
phases.says: Cut the bar first and then colour. Which number says how it was cut?
phases.check: Away from the screen: rule a bar into nine equal parts, colour five, and tell me which of your two numbers you wrote down first and why that one.
phases.feels: the bar is cut before anything is coloured, so the lower number is already there and waiting
phases.hands: On squared paper rule a long bar and divide it into seven equal parts with a ruler before anything is coloured, counting the parts out loud on the empty bar. Then colour four of them. Write the fraction underneath the bar rather than beside it, and read it back from the bottom up in two halves: cut into seven equal parts, and four of them taken.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many cuts are drawn across your bar? Second rung, the phase's: how many of its pieces did you colour in? Third rung: the bar is cut back to four parts with one of them filled and the two slots are built on that before the longer bar comes back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a written line is read from its left hand end, so the number met first looks like the number that goes first, and the upper slot is the slot the eye reaches first as well.
wrong.move: writes the seven on top and the four underneath, because the seven is the number the sentence gives first.
wrong.screen: the counting pass runs on the slots exactly as the child filled them. The lower slot asks for four and only four of the seven cut lines are ticked before it is satisfied, leaving three pieces of the bar outside the count altogether, and the upper slot then asks for seven coloured pieces and runs out after four. The child's two tiles stay exactly where they were dropped, a second bar cut into seven is drawn beneath the first with four of its parts filled, and the two bars are left standing together.

wrong.why: the coloured pieces and the plain ones are the two heaps on the mat, and two numbers look as though they ought to name that pair.
wrong.move: counts the pieces left over instead of the pieces the bar was cut into, and writes four over three.
wrong.screen: the counting pass runs twice over the same bar with nothing cleared. The first pass counts only the plain pieces and stops at three; the second runs along the whole bar and counts seven, the four filled ones included, with the bracket spanning the whole bar drawn green above it. The lower slot is read out as the count under that bracket, and the three the child wrote is left standing beside it so the two counts can be held against each other.

phases.screen: one uncut bar, the cutter dial above it and two empty fraction slots below
phases.soWhat: The lower number says how many equal parts the whole was cut into, and the upper number says how many of them are being counted.

phases.win: the naming slot refuses the label, an even cut is drawn beside the uneven one, and the name lands only once the pieces match
phases.does: slides the cut until the two pieces plainly differ, then tries to name one
phases.goal: pieces that are not equal have no fraction name
phases.says: Slide the cut until the pieces look wrong. Now try to call one of them a quarter.
phases.check: Somebody cuts a cake into six pieces of different sizes and calls one of them a sixth. What would you say to them, and why?
phases.feels: four pieces, and not one of them has a name until all four of them match
phases.hands: Fold one paper square into four equal parts and colour one of them. Then take a second square of exactly the same size, fold it carelessly into four pieces that plainly differ, and colour the largest. Lay the two coloured pieces on top of one another and ask whether both of them can be called a quarter.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: are your pieces all the same size? Second rung, the phase's: what does the word quarter promise about the four pieces? Third rung: the strip is cut evenly into two and the child names one piece, then the same cut is slid off centre and they try that same name again. Nothing is ever marked wrong and the word pad stays open.

wrong.why: counting the pieces is the move that has worked on every bar so far, and four pieces look like quarters however carelessly they were cut.
wrong.move: calls one of four unequal pieces a quarter, because there are four pieces lying on the mat.
wrong.screen: the slot refuses the tile and prints what is wrong with the picture rather than what the answer is. An evenly cut copy of the same strip is drawn directly beneath from the same left edge, and the long piece is slid down onto the small ones, where it covers two of them exactly. The strip is then read out as five pieces of that smaller size, so each small piece is one fifth of it, and the child's own cut stays exactly where it was slid to.

wrong.why: a picture that looks even reads as even, and nothing on a page measures anything for you unless you make it.
wrong.move: nudges the cut until the two pieces look about right and names them halves without measuring anything.
wrong.screen: the two pieces are lifted off the strip and laid one on top of the other, where the longer one overhangs by the amount it overhangs by. A measuring bar runs along each and prints its length, and the naming slot stays shut while the two lengths differ. The moment the cut is slid until the two measure the same the slot opens by itself and the word half goes in, and no tile is ever moved for the child.

phases.screen: a bar with one free cut line resting a little off its middle
phases.soWhat: Pieces that are not equal have no fraction name at all, so equal parts are part of the meaning rather than a rule about neatness.
phases.concept: Equal parts, or no fraction at all

phases.win: every card settles in each tray it earns, and the cards sharing a lower number are drawn together
phases.does: drops each written fraction into every tray its two numbers earn
phases.goal: a fraction is sorted by comparing its two numbers
phases.says: Look at the number on top and the one below. Which trays does this card belong in?
phases.check: Look at 6/6. Which trays does it belong in, and which test did you use to put it in each one?
phases.feels: one card, three trays open at once, and not one of the three is wrong
phases.hands: Write 5/9, 11/8, 1/9 and 8/8 on four cards and set out five labelled paper trays, proper, improper, like, unlike and unit. Let each card be dropped into every tray it earns, with the test said out loud each time, and do not let a card be put down until all five tests have been tried on it.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which of the two numbers on this card is the larger? Second rung, the phase's: is the upper one smaller than the lower one, or is it not? Third rung: the shelf is cut to two trays, proper and improper, and the whole stack is sorted on that one test before the other three trays open again. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: improper has been heard as top heavy, and a card whose two numbers match does not look top heavy at all.
wrong.move: leaves 8/8 out of the improper tray, because its two numbers are the same rather than one of them being bigger.
wrong.screen: the test is printed above the tray in the words it is actually written in, numerator greater than or equal to denominator, with greater and equal lit one after the other as separate ways of passing. The card is then drawn out on the mat behind the shelf: a whole cut into eight parts with eight of them filled leaves nothing amber anywhere and the green bracket spanning the whole sits exactly over the filled run, so the card is one whole. The child's sorting is left exactly as it was and no card is moved for them.

wrong.why: five trays and a stack of cards look like a matching game, and one card in one tray is what matching has always meant.
wrong.move: drops each card into one tray only, as though a fraction had to pick a single kind and stay in it.
wrong.screen: each card is lifted in turn and every one of the five tests is run on it with the trays it passes lighting together rather than one at a time. On 1/9 three trays light at once, because its upper number is the smaller one, its upper number is one, and it shares a lower number with 5/9 standing in the stack beside it. Every card the child has already placed stays where it was put and the further trays it earns are simply drawn open beside it.

phases.screen: the shelf of five labelled trays with a stack of written fractions beside it
phases.soWhat: Each of the five kinds is a separate test on the two numbers of the fraction, so one fraction can belong to several of them at the same time.
phases.concept: The five kinds, sorted by their two numbers

phases.win: the pieces close back into one whole and the three fractions are written under them
phases.does: cuts one half in two, names the new pieces, and slides everything back into a whole
phases.goal: two quarters make a half and four quarters make a whole
phases.says: Cut one half in two. What is each of the new pieces called?
phases.check: Away from the screen: how many quarters are there in three halves, and how did you work that out?
phases.feels: a half and two quarters, three pieces of two different sizes, and they still close back into one whole
phases.hands: Fold a paper circle in half and cut along the fold. Cut one of the two halves in half again and lay the three pieces out in a row. Ask for each piece to be named before anything is slid back, then push the three together and ask what they come to.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many pieces of this size would it take to fill the whole circle? Second rung, the phase's: how many of them cover the piece that was never cut? Third rung: the circle is cut in half only, and the two pieces are named before either of them is cut again. Nothing already named is renamed for the child.

wrong.why: they were made by halving something, and the word that names the action is the word nearest to hand when the pieces have to be named.
wrong.move: calls the two smaller pieces halves, because they were cut out of a half.
wrong.screen: the two small pieces are laid onto the untouched half and two of them cover it exactly, so the half is redrawn as two of that size standing side by side. The whole circle is then rebuilt and the same piece is laid onto it, where four of that size are needed to fill it and the count is drawn out one piece at a time. The names the child wrote stay printed under their pieces and the new naming is written underneath rather than over them.

wrong.why: three pieces in a row look like three of something, and a whole cut into three parts is where thirds come from.
wrong.move: counts the three pieces lying on the mat and calls each of them a third.
wrong.screen: a circle of exactly the same size is drawn beside the child's and ruled into three genuinely equal parts. The half is laid over one of those thirds and hangs past it, and each of the two quarters is laid over one and falls short of it. The refusal from the second phase is printed again underneath, that pieces which are not all the same size have no single name, and the child's three labels stay on the mat throughout.

phases.screen: one whole already cut in half, with one of the halves waiting
phases.soWhat: Two quarters make a half, two halves make a whole, and four quarters make a whole.
phases.concept: Halves and quarters in one field

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the moment cut again lands on one of the two halves. The piece opens along a single drawn line into two, and every label on the mat rewrites itself in the same movement: the untouched piece still reads as a half, and the two new ones come up as quarters while the bracket spanning the whole circle stays green and stays exactly the size it was. Then the three pieces slide back together and close into one circle with no seam showing, and the three fractions are written in a row underneath, a half and a quarter and a quarter, with the whole drawn whole above them. Push a finger against the closed circle and it opens again into the same three pieces, so the cutting and the closing can be run back and forth as often as a hand likes. Nothing else on the mat moves and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase one uncut bar lies across the middle of the mat with the cutter dial resting above it and two empty fraction slots waiting underneath, one over the other with their rule already drawn between them. On the second a bar carries a single free cut line sitting a little off its middle, so the two pieces plainly differ before anything has been touched. On the third the shelf of five labelled trays runs along the foot with a stack of written fraction cards squared up beside it and the mat above them empty. On the fourth one whole circle lies already cut in half, the two halves drawn apart by the width of the cut, with the cut again control lit beside the nearer of them. The running count at the top left holds the parts coloured against the parts the whole was cut into, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the uncut bar, or the free cut line, or the top card of the stack, or the half nearest the control, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how this whole has been divided. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any whole, any number of even cuts up to twenty, with the free cut line, the collection view and the sorting shelf switched on or off. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on naming the two numbers, refusing an uneven cut, sorting fractions into the five kinds, and building halves and quarters out of one whole.
voiceLines: One whole thing on the mat. Cut it into equal parts before you colour anything.
Cut the bar first and then colour. Which number says how it was cut?
Slide the cut until the pieces look wrong. Now try to call one of them a quarter.
Look at the number on top and the one below. Which trays does this card belong in?
Cut one half in two. What is each of the new pieces called?
Another whole. How many equal parts is this one going into?
Free play. Any whole, any number of cuts, with the free cut line and the trays as you like.
Count the cuts first and the coloured pieces second. The mat is still showing both.
Every whole cut, every part named, and the pieces nobody took still lying on the mat.

observations.why: The lower number counts how the whole was divided, and the dividing happens before anything is taken.
observations.soWhat: Read a fraction from the bottom up, because a piece has to have a size before there is anything to count.
observations.observe: The cuts went in before any colour did, and the lower number could be counted on a bar with nothing filled.

observations.why: A fraction names a part of a whole, so the whole has to be there for the name to be against anything.
observations.soWhat: A coloured piece on its own has lost the thing that gave it its name.
observations.observe: The pieces nobody took stayed on the mat, full size, for the whole of every phase.

observations.why: A quarter means one of four pieces that are all the same size, and these four were not.
observations.soWhat: Equal is part of what a fraction means, and not a tidiness rule added on afterwards.
observations.observe: With the cut slid off centre, no label would go into the slot at all.

observations.why: Proper, like and unit are three separate tests, and they are all run on the same two numbers.
observations.soWhat: The five kinds are not five boxes to choose between, so a fraction may answer to several of them.
observations.observe: One card landed in three trays at once and nothing on the shelf objected.

source_tool.description: One whole thing lies in the middle of the stage, a bar or a circle or a row of separate counters, with a cutter above it and an empty fraction waiting underneath. A dial sets how many equal parts the cutter makes, and the cuts are drawn before anything is coloured, so the lower number can always be counted whether or not any part has been taken. Tapping a part colours it and it joins the count; the parts nobody took stay on the stage, drawn in full, because a part with no whole beside it has lost the thing that names it. The fraction underneath is built by dragging the two numbers into their slots, and the slots are read back against the picture rather than marked. A free cut control replaces the even cutter with a line the child can slide, so the pieces can be made deliberately unequal: the naming slot then refuses every label and says what is wrong with the picture, which is the only way the word equal gets any work to do. A collection view swaps the single cut whole for a row of separate things of the same kind, so one written fraction is seen to serve both. Along the foot runs a shelf of five labelled trays, and a stack of written fractions is sorted onto it: a card may sit in more than one tray, and cards sharing a lower number are drawn side by side when they land.
source_tool.art_direction: One whole on a cutting mat, five trays below / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: bars and circles that are cut, paper strips laid from a common left edge, bowls that fill, trays with printed labels, loose parts that slide, and a rail with named gates along it.
A part is never drawn without its whole. Wherever a fraction is shown, the whole it came from stays in the same frame, entire, with the parts nobody took still drawn and still countable.

Every division into parts is made by a drawn cut, a score line or a gap, never by a change of colour alone. The cuts go in before any fill does, so the lower number can be counted whether anything is coloured or not.

Where a fraction says its parts are equal, every part of that whole is drawn the same size and the same shape. Where a stage deliberately shows unequal pieces, it says so in its own label and no fraction name is written against them.

A fraction is always written with its upper number above a level horizontal line and its lower number below it, both upright and centred. The line is never slanted and the two numbers are never set side by side. A mixed number is drawn as an upright whole number beside a stacked fraction.

Two fractions shown to be the same amount are drawn as strips of identical length and width, laid one directly under the other from one common left edge, so that the filled parts ending in the same place is what carries the claim.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most twenty things, separated, large enough to count at a glance and never overlapping.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a part, a strip or a token the child is counting, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The parts a fraction counts are deep blue, the parts of that same whole which it leaves are amber, and a whole shown entire or a bracket spanning one whole is green, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. A second writing of an amount already on the stage is rose, so an equivalent fraction is told from the fraction it came from without either being called wrong. The greater of two fractions one of the two rules can settle is vermilion, and a pair that neither rule settles is sky blue, which is how the stage says undecided without saying wrong. All of that holds in greyscale, because a part is told from the rest by the cut line between them and by its label before it is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the cuts first and the coloured pieces second. The mat is still showing both.
voice.onNext: Another whole. How many equal parts is this one going into?
voice.opening: One whole thing on the mat. Cut it into equal parts before you colour anything.
voice.onFinish: Every whole cut, every part named, and the pieces nobody took still lying on the mat.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any whole, any number of cuts, with the free cut line and the trays as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Equal parts, or no fraction at all
The five kinds, sorted by their two numbers
Halves and quarters in one field

placement.where: Straight after a paper square has been folded into equal parts and coloured by hand, and before any fraction is written on the board. The tool is what lets an uneven cut be tried on purpose and refused on the spot, which a folded paper cannot say for itself.

answer_key.rule: The lower number says how many equal parts the whole was cut into, and the upper number says how many of those parts are being counted. Read a fraction from the bottom up, because a piece has to have a size before there is anything to count. The parts must be equal or there is no fraction to name them at all. The same written fraction serves one thing cut up and a group of separate things. A fraction is proper when its upper number is the smaller one, improper when its upper number is greater than or equal to its lower one, and a unit fraction when its upper number is one. Two fractions are like when they share a lower number and unlike when they do not. Two quarters make a half, two halves make a whole, and four quarters make a whole.
answer_key.wrong: The picture is drawn again beside the writing and the two are counted together: the cuts first, then the coloured parts. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The ribbon was cut into seven equal pieces, so seven is the number below the line.
Four of those pieces were tied together, so four is the number above the line.
Read from the bottom up: seven equal pieces, four of them taken, which is 4/7.
items.answer: 4/7, where the seven counts the equal pieces and the four counts the pieces tied together
items.question: A ribbon is cut into seven equal pieces and four of them are tied together. Write that as a fraction and say what each number counts.
items.checkpoint: The lower number cuts the whole and the upper number counts what was taken from it.
items.misconception: Writing 7/4 because seven was the number mentioned first.

steps: A quarter means one of four equal parts of the whole strip.
These four pieces are not equal, so none of them is one of four equal parts.
There is no fraction name for any of these pieces until the strip is cut again into equal parts.
items.answer: No, because a quarter has to be one of four pieces that are all the same size
items.question: A paper strip is cut into four pieces, but one piece is twice as long as each of the others. Can one of the small pieces be called a quarter?
items.checkpoint: Equal parts are part of what a fraction means, not an extra tidiness rule.
items.misconception: Calling any one of four pieces a quarter because there happen to be four of them.

steps: A proper fraction has the smaller number on top, which is true of 5/9 and of 1/9.
An improper fraction has a numerator greater than or equal to its denominator, so 11/8 and 8/8 both qualify, and 8/8 is exactly one whole.
Like fractions share a lower number, so 5/9 and 1/9 are the like pair, and a unit fraction has one on top, which is 1/9.
items.answer: 5/9 and 1/9 are proper, 11/8 and 8/8 are improper, 5/9 and 1/9 are like fractions, and 1/9 is a unit fraction
items.question: Look at 5/9, 11/8, 1/9 and 8/8. Say which are proper, which are improper, which two are like fractions, and which is a unit fraction.
items.checkpoint: Every one of the five kinds is decided by comparing the two numbers of the fraction.
items.misconception: Leaving 8/8 out of the improper tray because the two numbers are the same rather than one being bigger.

steps: Cutting the bread in two equal parts makes halves, so the untouched piece is one half.
Cutting one half into two equal parts makes quarters, so the two smaller pieces are each a quarter.
Two quarters make a half, so a half and two quarters make two halves, which is one whole.
items.answer: One half, one quarter and one quarter, and together they make one whole flatbread
items.question: A flatbread is cut in half and one half is cut in half again. Name the three pieces and say what they come to together.
items.checkpoint: Two quarters make a half, two halves make a whole, and four quarters make a whole.
items.misconception: Calling the two smaller pieces halves because they came out of a half.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A wall is painted in nine equal bands and five of them are blue. What fraction of the wall is blue, and what does the nine count?
items.final_answer: 5/9, and the nine counts the equal bands the wall was divided into

items.question: In 7/12, which number counts the parts that were taken, and where is it written?
items.final_answer: The seven, and it is written above the line

items.question: A cake is cut into six pieces of different sizes. Is one of them a sixth?
items.final_answer: No, because sixths have to be six pieces that are all the same size

items.question: Two children each cut an identical sheet into four pieces. One makes four equal pieces and the other makes four unequal ones. Whose picture can be labelled one quarter?
items.final_answer: Only the one with four equal pieces, because the other sheet has no piece that is one of four equal parts

items.question: Which of 4/11, 13/6, 1/11 and 6/6 are improper fractions?
items.final_answer: 13/6 and 6/6, because in each the upper number is greater than or equal to the lower one

items.question: From 2/15, 1/8 and 9/15, name the two like fractions and the unit fraction.
items.final_answer: 2/15 and 9/15 are the like fractions, because both are written in fifteenths, and 1/8 is the unit fraction

items.question: A field is split into two equal halves and one half is split equally again. Write the three pieces as fractions and show that they make one whole field.
items.final_answer: One half, one quarter and one quarter, and 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2, so the three pieces are two halves, which is one whole

items.question: How many quarters are there in three halves?
items.final_answer: Six quarters, because each half is two quarters and three halves is six of them

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: cuts the whole into that many equal parts and draws every cut
colours a part and adds it to the count above the line
replaces the even cutter with a line the child can slide off centre
opens the two fraction slots and reads them back against the picture
swaps the cut whole for a row of separate things of one kind
opens the five labelled trays and the stack of written fractions
cuts one chosen part in two and renames every piece

teaching_notes: Fold a paper square into equal parts and colour some of them by hand before the tool is opened, and write the fraction underneath the folded square rather than beside it, so the picture and the writing are read together from the start. Then use the tool for the thing paper cannot do. Go to the free cut early and make the pieces plainly unequal on purpose, and ask the class to name one of them. The refusal is the teaching, and it is worth waiting for somebody to argue about. Insist on reading every fraction from the bottom up, out loud, in two halves: the whole was cut into this many equal parts, and this many were taken. A class that reads the lower number first has already stopped comparing the two numbers as though they were separate. Use the collection view once the cut whole is secure, because a child who has only ever seen a shaded circle will not recognise the same fraction in a row of counters. The sorting shelf is where the recap work belongs: let a card sit in two trays at once, and do not rush the card that is improper because its two numbers are equal, which is the one the class will leave out. The thirteen vocabulary words of the chapter can be made into cards from this shelf, one word to a tray, and quizzed in pairs.
generation_prompt: Build a fraction naming tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. One whole thing sits in the middle of the working area, switchable between a long bar, a circle and a row of separate counters. A cutter dial above it sets how many equal parts the whole is divided into, from two to twenty, and every cut is drawn as a near-black line before anything is filled, so the parts stay countable while empty. Tapping a part fills it and raises the count above the line; untaken parts stay drawn in full and are never faded or cropped. Below the whole sits an empty fraction, an upper slot and a lower slot separated by a level horizontal rule, filled by dragging number tiles. When both slots are filled the tool draws a counting pass over the picture, ticking the cuts against the lower slot and the filled parts against the upper one, without marking anything right or wrong. A free cut control replaces the even cutter with a single draggable line: while the two pieces differ in size the naming slots refuse every tile and print the reason, and an evenly cut copy of the same whole is drawn beside it for comparison. A collection view swaps the cut whole for a row of identical separate things, keeping the same fraction underneath. Along the foot runs a shelf of five labelled trays reading proper, improper, like, unlike and unit, with a stack of written fraction cards beside it; a card may be dropped into more than one tray, a wrong tray slides the card back and lights the two numbers being compared, and cards sharing a lower number are drawn shoulder to shoulder when they land. A cut again control divides one chosen part in two and relabels every piece. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Cut the whole first, then colour the parts you are taking. Count the cuts for the number below the line. Count the coloured parts for the number above it. If the pieces are not equal, no name will fit. On the shelf, a card may belong in more than one tray.
